sections.title: Recognition
sections.text: This small to medium waxcap has a usually conical cap, sometimes expanded with a central umbo, coloured yellow, orange or red. Its waxy gills are pale to lemon-yellow and often ascend toward the stem, where they are free or narrowly attached. The slender stem is yellow to orange, paler at the base and lacks a ring. The cap and other parts turn grey and then black with age or after damage; the spore print is white.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: It grows on the ground in unfertilised lawns and grasslands, as well as on fixed dunes, banks and roadside verges. Fruiting is mainly in summer and autumn in north-western Europe; local climate shifts the season.

sections.title: Similar species and species complex
sections.text: Hygrocybe conica is a complex of related taxa whose boundaries are not fully resolved. The dune-associated H. conicoides may have more orange gills and blacken more slowly; H. punicea can look similar in colour but does not blacken. Colour alone is therefore not enough for identification, and some cases require closer mycological examination.

sections.title: Food safety
sections.text: Do not eat. The DGfM lists H. conica among species associated with a gastrointestinal syndrome. Reports attributed to this species appear rare and the identification may be uncertain, but that caveat does not establish it as edible. An illustration or remote identification is not enough to determine that a mushroom is safe.

traits: Cap generally 1.5–7 cm, conical then sometimes expanded with a central umbo; yellow, orange or red, viscid in wet weather, blackening with age or after damage
Waxy gills, initially pale to lemon-yellow and sometimes becoming more orange; they blacken and are free or very narrowly attached to the stem
Stem 4–10 cm, yellow to orange with a paler base, without a ring; initially solid, it gradually blackens
Whitish to yellowish flesh that blackens quickly when cut; white spore print
Unfertilised lawns and grasslands, fixed dunes and grassy banks · mainly summer and autumn
The name Hygrocybe conica is used for a taxonomically complex group; boundaries among related taxa remain debated
safetyNote: Do not eat: the DGfM lists Hygrocybe conica among species associated with a gastrointestinal syndrome. Published cases appear rare and attribution may be uncertain; caution is warranted, especially as the name covers a group of closely related species.
